items.title: NativeHTMLKit
items.text:
Native desktop windows from HTML and CSS, driven by Python, PowerShell or a shell script. No browser engine, no JavaScript, no local web server: a small Rust host renders your page and sends your program the user's events over a private local connection.

Real capture: the Python UI gallery on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland (Core 1.0.3, Python SDK 0.1.2, UI 0.1.1). See Screenshots and media for every example.

items.title: Start here
items.text:
• Getting started: install one package and open your first window in five minutes, in Python, PowerShell or Bash.
  • Tutorials: build complete apps step by step: a notes app, an expense tracker, a process dashboard, a settings editor, a Git branch picker.
  • How-to guides: recipes for events, forms, dialogs, multiple windows, background work, live charts, styling, distribution and troubleshooting.
  • Concepts: how the host, your script and the page fit together, and why.
  • Reference: where each package documents its exact API, plus the capability matrix, limitations, glossary and FAQ.

items.title: A complete app in a few lines
items.text:
examples/getting-started/five_lines.py
# The smallest NativeHTMLKit app (home page sample). Run: python five_lines.py
from nativehtmlkit import Application

with Application.start(name="Hello") as app:
    window = app.open_html('<h1 id="title">Hello</h1><button id="go">Click me</button>')
    window.document.on("click", lambda e: window.document.set_text("title", "Clicked!"), element="go")
    app.run()

The quick start explains each line (including why the script runs twice) and the same app in PowerShell uses Start-NativeHTMLKitScript.

items.title: Tested examples
items.text: Every code sample on this site is a file in examples/, and a committed harness runs each one against the released packages in the host's headless test mode before the documentation is published. See Examples and verification.

items.title: What it is not
items.text: NativeHTMLKit is not a web browser, not a web UI framework and not a plugin platform. It runs no JavaScript, loads nothing from the network, and implements a documented CSS profile rather than the whole web platform. If you need arbitrary web content, a browser-based toolkit is the better fit; see Why native?.

items.title: Limitations and qualifications
items.text: This page lists what the released packages (Core 1.0.3, CLI 0.1.2, Python SDK 0.1.2, PowerShell SDK 0.1.2, UI 0.1.1) do not do, or do only with qualifications. For per-feature availability see the matrix. A feature appearing in source code is not automatic proof of support on every OS/runtime combination.

items.title: Platforms and runtimes
items.text:
• Targets: Linux with KDE Plasma on Wayland, and Windows x64. macOS is not a target of the current releases.
  • Python SDK on Linux: the released x64 wheel uses a manylinux_2_39_x86_64 tag. Systems with glibc older than 2.39 do not meet that wheel's compatibility floor; the source package has no native host.
  • PowerShell: Windows PowerShell 5.1 is Windows only. Linux uses PowerShell 7.2+.

items.title: UI library
items.text:
• Version: NativeHTMLKit UI 0.1.1 is an early (pre-1.0) release with a deliberately small component set. Its 0.1.1 packages passed the real-input GUI suite at 100% scaling against Python SDK 0.1.2 / PowerShell SDK 0.1.2 / Core 1.0.3 on KDE Plasma Wayland (Python, PowerShell 7) and Windows Server 2022 (Python, PowerShell 7, Windows PowerShell 5.1). IME, 125/150% scaling and screen-reader checks were last run against UI 0.1.0 with SDK 0.1.0 / Core 1.0.2.
  • Fixed tree: components are declared before mounting; afterwards only bound state changes the page. Lists are text-only (text_list / Add-NHKUiTextList).
  • Reactive state: Python Computed can race when multiple threads mutate its dependencies concurrently. Avoid such concurrent patterns until fixed; update related state from one thread.
  • Lifecycle: repeatedly creating and disposing UI windows can accumulate shutdown callbacks; limit repeated create/dispose loops until fixed.
  • No modal wrapper: HTML dialogs, native file dialogs, extra windows, clipboard and live bitmaps are SDK calls made next to the UI library.

items.title: Accessibility
items.text:
• Core 1.0.3 has a reported Linux Orca collapsed-select announcement issue (NHK-CROSS-0010).
  • UI-specific screen-reader coverage remains incomplete. See accessibility basics.

items.title: Headless test mode
items.text:
With NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 (SDKs) or NATIVEHTMLKIT_CLI_TEST_HEADLESS=1 (CLI) the host runs the protocol without a window. In that mode:

  • there is no synthetic user input — only document operations you call (for example request_submit, which fires submit, or replace_control_range, which fires input) produce events; set_value, set_checked and set_selected_values fire none;
  • the clipboard and native file/folder dialogs are unavailable and fail with RPC error -32001;
  • opening external targets and revealing files are unavailable;
  • desktop preferences report no observed values.

Headless runs prove startup, rendering, DOM state, readiness and clean shutdown — not real input, focus, IME or screen-reader behaviour.

items.title: Not included
items.text: JavaScript and browser APIs, network resource loading, an HTTP server, a general-purpose plugin framework, a UI modal wrapper, web-style routing, video/audio playback, and full Chrome-level HTML/CSS support.

items.title: Concepts
items.text:
These pages explain why NativeHTMLKit behaves the way it does. They contain no step-by-step instructions; for those see the tutorials and how-to guides.

Page Read it when you want to understand… Architecture which component owns windows, rendering, language APIs and UI helpers Process and lifecycle model why your script runs twice, what ready and shutdown mean, how quitting is negotiated Threading and callbacks where your callbacks run, what may block, how to do background work safely Documents and stale handles windows vs documents, why an old handle suddenly raises a stale error Security model what is trusted, what is escaped, what the host refuses Why native? the trade-offs compared with Electron or an embedded browser

All statements describe the released packages: Core 1.0.3, CLI 0.1.2, Python SDK 0.1.2, PowerShell SDK 0.1.2 and UI 0.1.1.

items.title: Architecture — who owns what?
items.text:
flowchart TD
  APP[Your Python or PowerShell program] --> UI[UI library, optional<br/>nativehtmlkit_ui / NativeHTMLKit.UI]
  APP --> SDK[Language SDK<br/>nativehtmlkit / NativeHTMLKit]
  UI --> SDK
  SHELL[Shell script or pipeline] --> CLI[Native CLI<br/>nativehtmlkit / nhk]
  SDK -->|wire protocol v1<br/>local authenticated IPC| HOST[Core native host<br/>nativehtmlkit-host, Rust]
  CLI -->|wire protocol v1| HOST
  HOST --> OS[Linux KDE Wayland / Windows desktop]

NativeHTMLKit is not a website in a hidden browser tab. A Rust native host parses HTML and CSS, lays out and draws the page, owns the native windows, handles keyboard, pointer, IME, accessibility and native dialogs, and reports events to your program. Your program — the backend — contains the application logic and sends commands such as “set this element's text” back to the host.

items.title: Components
items.text:
Component Owns Does not own Core (nativehtmlkit-host) Native windows, HTML/CSS engine, input, rendering, native dialogs, clipboard, live bitmaps, the wire protocol Application logic, language APIs Python SDK (nativehtmlkit) Python API for applications, windows, documents, nodes, bitmaps; launching the bundled host; diagnostics Rendering, widgets PowerShell SDK (NativeHTMLKit) The same host-level features as exported functions; the event pump and background tasks for PowerShell Rendering, widgets UI library (nativehtmlkit_ui, NativeHTMLKit.UI) Reactive state, computed values, a compact component set (layout, text, buttons, inputs, select, checkbox, lists, conditional regions) and themes Anything the SDK does not expose; native dialogs, extra windows and bitmaps stay SDK calls CLI (nativehtmlkit, alias nhk) select, view, form and doctor commands for shell pipelines, with a stdin/stdout/exit-status contract General event subscription or scripting

Each SDK wheel/module and the CLI archive ship the native host they were released with, so a normal install needs no separate Core download.

items.title: The boundary rule
items.text:
• The UI libraries call only the public API of their language SDK. They never talk to Core directly. Your application can mix both: build the main window with the UI library and use the SDK for file dialogs, clipboard, a second window or a live bitmap.
  • The CLI is independent of the language SDKs: it implements its own protocol v1 client and bundles its own host.
  • A feature that Core does not expose cannot be added in a UI library or an application through private calls; it belongs in Core and the SDKs.

items.title: The wire protocol
items.text:
SDKs and the CLI talk to the host over a private local channel (a Unix-domain socket on Linux, a named pipe on Windows), authenticated with a per-launch token. Messages are length-prefixed JSON-RPC 2.0. Protocol v1 is the public, stable contract since Core 1.0.3: within v1, framing, method and operation names, parameter names and types, error codes and lifecycle ordering never change; new methods, operations, optional parameters and result members may be added, and clients must ignore what they do not know. The authoritative description is the Core protocol README.

Most applications never see the protocol: they use the SDK. Low-level escape hatches exist (Document.command(op, ...) in Python, Invoke-NativeHTMLKitDocumentCommand in PowerShell) for documented document operations that have no convenience wrapper.

items.title: Windows and documents
items.text:
A window is a native top-level window owned by the host. It shows at most one document: the HTML you loaded with app.open_html(...) / window.load_html(...) / window.load_file(...) in Python, or Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml / Open-NativeHTMLKitFile in PowerShell. Loading new HTML into the same window atomically replaces its document; unloading (doc.unload() / Remove-NativeHTMLKitDocument) leaves the window open and empty.

An inline HTML source is limited to 1 MiB. Relative stylesheet, image and font URLs resolve against an asset root: the folder of a loaded file, or the folder you pass as asset_root / -AssetRoot.

items.title: Handles are generation-bound
items.text:
Every object the SDK gives you — Window, Document, Node, live bitmap, event subscription — refers to one specific host object. The host gives each document a new identity (generation) when it is loaded, so a handle can never silently point at a different page.

A document handle becomes stale when:

  • its window loaded another document (the old document handle is retired, the new one is live),
  • the document was unloaded,
  • its window closed, or
  • the application shut down (app.shutdown retires every window and document handle at once).

Using a stale handle fails locally, before anything is sent:

Python PowerShell Stale window or document nativehtmlkit.StaleDocumentError (a StaleHandleError) NativeHTMLKit.StaleObjectException App is shutting down (new window/document refused) ApplicationShutdownError — (handles are already retired) The host itself reports a gone object RpcError with code == -32004 NativeHTMLKit.RpcException with Code -32004 Operation no longer valid (invalid state, e.g. during shutdown) RpcError with code == -32008 NativeHTMLKit.RpcException with Code -32008

The UI libraries treat these errors as “the document is gone” and dispose themselves quietly instead of reporting a corrupted UI.

Practical rule: after replacing a document, re-register event handlers on the new document object, and never cache document handles in long-lived workers without handling the stale error. Handlers, nodes and bitmaps of the old document are released with it.

items.title: Elements, ids and nodes
items.text:
Most commands address an element by its HTML id (doc.set_text("status", "…"), Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText -Element status). For elements without an id, doc.query_nodes(selector) / Get-NativeHTMLKitNodes return opaque node references that are bound to the same document generation; they become stale with it. doc.query(selector) returns only the ids of matching elements that have one.

Several changes can be applied as one host transaction with doc.batch([...]) / Invoke-NativeHTMLKitBatch.

items.title: Events and delegation
items.text:
Event handlers are registered on the document: doc.on("click", callback, element="save") / Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent -Type click -Element save. The event object carries the type, the nearest identified target element, and path — the ids of identified elements on the event's route. A handler registered with an element id fires when that id is the target or appears on the path, so one handler on a list container can serve all its rows (delegation). Without element, the handler receives every event of that type.

  • Events arrive after native dispatch. To stop a supported default action (for example a key's default editing), register it in advance with doc.prevent_default(...) / Set-NativeHTMLKitPreventDefault; a callback cannot cancel it afterwards.
  • Control events carry the current value / checked; key events carry key and code.
  • A document accepts at most 256 handlers.
  • Programmatic changes are not user input: set_value, set_checked and set_selected_values fire no events, while request_submit runs validation and fires invalid / submit, and replace_control_range goes through the native editor and fires input.

items.title: Live bitmaps
items.text:
A live bitmap (doc.create_bitmap(id, w, h) / New-NativeHTMLKitLiveBitmap) is a bounded RGBA8 image surface for <img src="ui4me-bitmap://ID">, shared with the host through a private memory-mapped file. Presenting a frame waits until the host has taken it, so there is no unbounded frame queue. A bitmap belongs to its document and is released when the document is replaced, unloaded or its window closes. See live bitmap charts.

Related: Update the page · Handle events · Threading and callbacks

items.title: Process and lifecycle model
items.text:
A NativeHTMLKit application is two cooperating processes: the native host, which owns the windows, and your script, which owns the logic. The SDK hides most of this, but knowing the model explains several rules you will meet in every tutorial.

sequenceDiagram
  participant L as Launcher run (python app.py / pwsh -File app.ps1)
  participant H as Native host
  participant B as Backend run (same script, second time)
  L->>H: start host with a private manifest
  H->>B: start the same script again, with endpoint + token
  B->>H: authenticate, create windows, load documents
  B->>H: app.ready
  Note over H,B: events flow to the backend, commands flow to the host
  H->>B: app.shutdown (last window closed or quit accepted)
  B-->>H: backend exits
  H-->>L: host exits; the launcher exits with the host's status

items.title: Your script runs twice
items.text:
When you run python app.py, Application.start() notices that it was not started by a host. It writes a private temporary manifest, starts the bundled host and waits; it never returns in that first run — the process ends with the host's exit status. The host then runs the same command again as its supervised backend. In that second run Application.start() connects to the host and returns the Application.

PowerShell works the same way: Start-NativeHTMLKitScript in a script run with pwsh -File app.ps1 (or powershell.exe -File app.ps1 on Windows) starts the host, which re-runs the script with the same PowerShell edition and arguments; the call returns the connected application only in the backend run. Script arguments are forwarded to the backend run.

Consequences:

  • Everything above Application.start() / Start-NativeHTMLKitScript runs twice. Keep imports, constants and function definitions there; put side effects (reading files, creating folders, network calls) below the call or inside main().
  • Python examples use if __name__ == "__main__": main() and keep work inside main().
  • Application.start() must run from a script file or python -m package.module; it refuses an interactive interpreter, python -c and standard input, because it could not re-run them. Command-line arguments are passed to the backend run unchanged.
  • A Python backend started with python -m nativehtmlkit run module:main (or by a host manifest) only connects; it is not relaunched.

items.title: Starting up: ready
items.text:
After connecting, the backend creates at least one window, loads its document and registers event handlers, then announces ready:

  • Python: app.run() sends ready and then waits for shutdown (or call app.ready() yourself earlier).
  • PowerShell: Set-NativeHTMLKitReady -Application $app (the UI library's Start-NHKUi does this for you unless you pass -NoReady), then Wait-NativeHTMLKit -Application $app -UntilShutdown.

The backend must authenticate and become ready before the manifest's startup deadline (startup_timeout_ms / -StartupTimeoutMilliseconds, default 30 seconds), otherwise the host gives up.

items.title: Single or multiple instances
items.text: instance="single" (Python) / -Instance single (PowerShell) is the default: launching the same app again forwards the launch to the running instance instead of opening a second copy. The identity is the app_id / -AppId (a reverse-DNS name such as org.example.Notes); without one, a stable identity is derived from the script path. Use "multiple" for tools where several copies make sense.

items.title: Closing windows and quitting
items.text:
Closing is a negotiation, because a window may have unsaved work:

  1. The user closes a window (or your code calls window.request_close() / Close-NativeHTMLKitWindow).
  2. If you installed a before-close policy (window.on_before_close(callback) / Set-NativeHTMLKitBeforeClose), the host asks it; returning false keeps the window open. In PowerShell the scriptblock's last output decides ($true allows).
  3. The window emits close_requested and then closed window events, and its handles become stale.

Quitting the whole application is negotiated the same way: app.request_quit() / Request-NativeHTMLKitQuit asks the before-quit policy (app.on_before_quit(callback) / Set-NativeHTMLKitBeforeQuit).

When the last window closes, or a quit is accepted, the host sends app.shutdown. In Core 1.0.x there is no closed window event for that last window — app.shutdown follows close_requested directly, and it implies that every window is closed. The SDKs therefore retire all window and document handles when shutdown arrives.

items.title: Shutting down
items.text:
• Python: app.run() delivers the events that arrived before app.shutdown (for up to two seconds), runs app.on_shutdown(...) callbacks in the thread that called run(), and returns normally. It raises DisconnectedError if the host disappeared instead of shutting down in order. Leaving the with Application.start(...) block closes the connection.
  • PowerShell: Wait-NativeHTMLKit -UntilShutdown returns after shutdown (or after your own Close-NativeHTMLKit) and throws NativeHTMLKit.DisconnectedException if the host vanished first. Put Close-NativeHTMLKit (and Stop-NHKUi) in a finally block.

After app.shutdown, the backend has the manifest's shutdown timeout (shutdown_timeout_ms, default 5 seconds) to finish and exit.

items.title: Exit status and teardown
items.text: The launcher exits with the host's status. If the Python launcher is interrupted by a signal it stops the host (bounded) and returns the conventional 128 + signal status, for example 143 for SIGTERM and 130 for Ctrl+C. The host supervises the backend, and the launcher keeps the host tied to its own lifetime (on Windows through a job object, on Linux by watching the launcher process), so stopping the launcher does not leave orphaned host or backend processes.

items.title: Headless test mode
items.text:
Set NATIVEHTMLKIT_TEST_MODE=1 before running a Python or PowerShell app, and the SDK starts the host with --headless (the CLI uses NATIVEHTMLKIT_CLI_TEST_HEADLESS=1). The host then runs the complete protocol and lifecycle — documents are parsed, styled and laid out, commands and queries work, events produced by document operations (for example request_submit firing submit, or replace_control_range firing input) are delivered — but no window is shown and:

  • there is no user input: nothing clicks or types for you;
  • the clipboard and native file dialogs are unavailable (the calls fail with RPC error -32001), as is opening external targets;
  • desktop preferences report no observed values.

Headless mode is meant for continuous integration and automated checks that an app starts, renders, reaches ready and shuts down cleanly. It never proves real input, focus or accessibility behaviour; those need an interactive desktop.

Related: Threading and callbacks · Documents and stale handles · Troubleshooting

items.title: Security model
items.text: NativeHTMLKit is a local desktop toolkit. Its security model is about keeping the host channel private, keeping untrusted text from becoming markup, and keeping the renderer away from the network and from arbitrary files.

items.title: A private, authenticated channel
items.text:
• The host creates a random token for each launch and gives the backend the endpoint and token through environment variables (UI4ME_ENDPOINT, UI4ME_TOKEN). The backend must authenticate with host.hello before anything else.
  • The endpoint is local only: a Unix-domain socket on Linux, a named pipe on Windows. On Linux the host's runtime files are created private to the user (directories 0700, files 0600).
  • The SDKs remove the connection variables from their own environment right after connecting, so programs your app starts do not inherit the secret and can launch their own NativeHTMLKit apps.
  • The launcher's temporary manifest (which names the program, script, arguments and working directory) lives in a private temporary folder — mode 0700 on Linux; on Windows the per-user temporary folder's permissions apply — and is removed when the launcher ends.

items.title: No JavaScript, no network
items.text:
There is no JavaScript engine, so <script> content and on… attributes do nothing. The resource loader always denies network URLs (http:, https:, ftp:, ws: …) as well as javascript: and blob: URLs for stylesheets, images and fonts. Pages can use:

  • local files inside the document's asset root (the folder of a loaded file, or the asset_root / -AssetRoot you pass) — paths outside every allowed root are refused before they are opened,
  • ui4me-res:// bundles you register from code, and ui4me-bitmap:// live bitmaps.

Activating a link is reported to your program as a link_activated event; what happens next is your code's decision (for example open_external).

items.title: Trusted and untrusted content
items.text:
The one rule you must follow: markup APIs take trusted HTML only.

Safe for any text (never parsed as HTML) Trusted markup only doc.set_text, Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText, doc.set_value, Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentValue, doc.set_attribute, UI text/heading/badge/alert/text_list and their PowerShell equivalents doc.replace_html, doc.insert_html, Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentHtml, open_html / Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml, UI raw_html / Add-NHKUiHtml

When you build HTML from data — file names, process names, user input, log lines — escape every value first: html.escape(value) in Python, [System.Net.WebUtility]::HtmlEncode($value) in PowerShell. Every tutorial and example on this site does this. The UI libraries escape all bound text and list items and reject unsafe attribute names (on…); generated element ids cannot be overridden.

items.title: Desktop services
items.text:
• open_external / Open-NativeHTMLKitExternal accepts only http, https, mailto and file URIs or absolute local paths. On Windows, local targets whose file type would be executed rather than opened (executables, scripts, shortcuts) are refused. Revealing a file requires a bounded absolute local path. Both are unavailable in headless mode.
  • Clipboard access is explicit (clipboard_text / set_clipboard_text, Get-/Set-NativeHTMLKitClipboard). Clipboard editing commands are deferred and report completion through events.

items.title: The CLI
items.text: nativehtmlkit select and view treat their stdin data as untrusted: it is escaped before display and bounded (UTF-8, up to 8 MiB, 2,000 rows and 32 columns in the 0.1.x line). The HTML passed to nativehtmlkit form --html and CSS passed with --css are trusted developer input — never feed them user-supplied content. Results are written to stdout only on success (exit 0). See the CLI reference.

items.title: What this model does not cover
items.text:
NativeHTMLKit runs with the permissions of the user who starts it; it is not a sandbox for untrusted code. Your Python or PowerShell program can do anything that user can. Treat example scripts like any other script you run.

Related: Architecture · Update the page · Distribute your app

items.title: Threading and callbacks
items.text: The host renders and handles input on its own threads; your program only receives events and sends commands. Where your callbacks run differs between Python and PowerShell, and it decides what you may block on.

items.title: Python SDK
items.text:
flowchart LR
  HOST[Native host] -- socket/pipe --> R[Receiver thread<br/>never runs your code]
  R --> Q[Ordered event queue]
  Q --> E[Event worker thread<br/>your document/window callbacks, in order]
  R --> C[Completion threads<br/>Future done-callbacks]
  R --> L[Lifecycle workers<br/>before_close / before_quit policies]
  M[Main thread] -->|app.run waits for shutdown| M
  • The transport reader never runs application code. Callbacks may therefore make synchronous calls to the host (doc.set_text(...) inside a click handler is normal).
  • Document and window events are delivered in order on one event worker thread. A slow handler delays every later event. The queue is bounded (128 queued notifications); events the SDK had to drop because a callback blocked are counted in app.rpc.dropped_notifications, and events the host dropped because the process stopped reading appear in app.host_diagnostics()["dropped_notifications"].
  • Close/quit policies are answered on separate request workers, so a busy event handler does not stall lifecycle control.
  • call_async futures complete on their own short-lived nativehtmlkit-completion thread. Done-callbacks may call the host synchronously or wait for other futures.
  • SDK calls are allowed from any thread, including your own threading.Thread workers. Use that for long work: compute in a worker and push results with doc.set_text(...) and friends.

Native dialogs inside an event handler. window.open_files(), save_file() and choose_folder() wait for the user by default (wait=True, no deadline). Called from an event handler, that blocks the event worker — every later click waits until the dialog closes. Pass wait=False to get a Future and handle the result in future.add_done_callback(...); future.cancel() asks the host to close the dialog. See file dialogs.

The optional async_adapter() exposes the same connection to an asyncio loop; it does not change who renders.

items.title: Python UI library
items.text:
• Build the component tree on the main thread before ui.mount(app); afterwards the tree is fixed and you change it only through state.
  • Each mounted UI has one owner thread that performs all runtime DOM writes. SDK event workers only enqueue events for it, and state changes are batched into few document updates.
  • State.set(...) may be called from any thread; bindings marshal the resulting DOM update to the owner. ui.post(fn, *args) runs a function on the owner thread (it raises if the bounded queue is full).
  • Known limitation: a computed(...) value can race when several threads change its dependencies at the same time. Change related state from one thread (for example, post results to the owner with ui.post). See limitations.
  • ui.diagnostics reports update counts, dropped events, errors and whether the DOM may be out of sync after a failed write.

items.title: PowerShell SDK
items.text:
PowerShell has one runspace per script and no background event thread. The SDK runs everything on your runspace through an event pump:

  • Wait-NativeHTMLKit -Application $app -UntilShutdown pumps messages and runs your scriptblocks until shutdown. Without -UntilShutdown it handles what is queued (waiting up to -TimeoutMilliseconds) and returns, which lets you write your own loop.
  • Every waiting SDK call also pumps. While a command such as Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText or a blocking Show-NativeHTMLKitFileDialog waits for its reply, host requests (close/quit policies) are still answered.
  • Callbacks never nest. A notification that arrives while one of your callbacks is running is deferred and delivered after it returns (up to 128 deferred notifications; further ones are dropped and counted). A blocking file dialog inside a click handler is therefore safe for lifecycle, but other clicks wait until it closes.
  • Callback nesting is limited to 32 levels; break/continue used outside a loop inside a callback is stopped at the callback boundary.

items.title: Scriptblock scope
items.text: A scriptblock written at script level resolves variables when it runs, in the script scope, so it can use $doc and a shared state object defined there. Assigning $count = $count + 1 inside a callback creates a local variable — keep mutable state in an object ($state.Count++). Inside a function, pass ({ ... }.GetNewClosure()) to capture the function's local variables. The UI library's -Data parameter passes context explicitly to -OnClick handlers instead.

items.title: Background work
items.text: Start-NativeHTMLKitTask -Application $app -ScriptBlock { ... } -ArgumentList ... -OnCompleted { ... } -OnFailed { ... } runs work in an isolated runspace without your variables or modules. Pass plain data only: SDK objects (application, window, document, bitmap, ...) are refused as arguments. -OnCompleted / -OnFailed run later on your runspace, during the normal pump and never inside another callback, so they may update the document. At most 8 tasks per application (32 per process) run at once; -TimeoutMilliseconds and Stop-NativeHTMLKitTask only request cancellation, and a worker that ignores it keeps its slot until it ends. Close-NativeHTMLKit requests stop of unfinished tasks and runs no further callbacks. See background work.

items.title: PowerShell UI library
items.text:
NativeHTMLKit.UI uses the same runspace. It records the owning runspace in Start-NHKUi and refuses updates from any other runspace — update state in -OnCompleted callbacks of SDK tasks, not inside the task scriptblock. Changes made inside an event callback are written in one batch when the callback returns; use Invoke-NHKUiBatch for many changes made elsewhere.

Related: Process and lifecycle model · Documents and stale handles

items.title: Why native instead of Electron or an embedded browser?
items.text: NativeHTMLKit targets local tools and small desktop applications where you want the familiar structure of HTML and CSS and the convenience of Python or PowerShell — without shipping a JavaScript engine, a browser process or a local web server.

items.title: What you gain
items.text:
• One language for the logic. Event handlers are ordinary Python functions or PowerShell scriptblocks. There is no front-end/back-end split, no bundler and no IPC layer for you to design.
  • Small, self-contained installs. The SDK wheel or module bundles the native host; pip install nativehtmlkit or Install-Module NativeHTMLKit is the whole runtime. The CLI is a single archive.
  • No network surface. There is no HTTP server and the renderer never fetches remote resources (see the security model).
  • Real native windows and services. Native file and folder dialogs, clipboard, multiple windows, window state, desktop preferences, accessibility integration and live RGBA bitmaps are host features, not browser emulations.
  • Scripts become apps. A PowerShell admin script or a shell pipeline can ask the user a question in a proper window (nativehtmlkit select, form) and continue with the answer.

items.title: What you give up
items.text:
• A subset of the web platform. The engine implements a large part of HTML and CSS layout, forms, dialogs and popovers, but it is not a complete browser. There are no JavaScript or browser APIs (fetch, canvas, web components, routing), no video/audio playback, and CSS support is defined by the engine's own profile and compatibility tests. Check the capability matrix and styling guide instead of assuming Chrome behaviour.
  • No existing web component ecosystem. React/Vue widgets, charting libraries in JavaScript and similar packages cannot run. Build charts with live bitmaps or server-free HTML/CSS.
  • Platform scope. The current targets are Linux with KDE Plasma on Wayland and Windows (x64). The Linux Python wheel needs glibc 2.39 or newer. See limitations.
  • Young UI library. nativehtmlkit_ui / NativeHTMLKit.UI 0.1.1 is an early release with a deliberately small component set.

items.title: When to choose something else
items.text:
• You need a complex single-page web application, existing JavaScript libraries, or exact browser rendering: use a browser-based stack.
  • You need macOS today: it is not a target of the current releases.
  • You need rich native widget toolkits (tree views with virtualization, docking, rich text editors): consider a native toolkit such as Qt.

If your app is a form, a dashboard, a picker, a settings dialog, a log viewer or a small utility written in Python or PowerShell, NativeHTMLKit is designed for exactly that. Start with Getting started.

items.title: Getting started
items.text: NativeHTMLKit shows native desktop windows whose content is plain HTML and CSS. Your program, written in Python or PowerShell (or a shell script using the CLI), owns the logic; a small native host process draws the window and sends you the user's events. There is no browser, no JavaScript and no local web server.

items.title: What happens when you run an app
items.text:
1. You run your script normally (python app.py, pwsh -File app.ps1).
  2. The SDK starts the bundled native host, and the host starts your script a second time as its backend, connected over a private local channel. That is why every example keeps its work after Application.start() / Start-NativeHTMLKitScript. See Process and lifecycle.
  3. Your code opens windows, loads HTML, subscribes to events and announces that it is ready.
  4. Events (clicks, typing, form submits) arrive in your callbacks; you change the page with document commands such as "set this element's text".
  5. When the user closes the last window, the host shuts the application down and your script ends.

items.title: Choose an entry point
items.text:
All entry points use the same native host and the same HTML/CSS renderer. They differ in who writes the page and how much control you get.

Your job Best entry point Why A Python program needs a window, and you are happy to write HTML Python SDK Full control: windows, documents, events, dialogs, clipboard, live bitmaps A Python tool needs a form-like window quickly Python UI Reactive state()/computed(), inputs, lists and layout without writing HTML A PowerShell admin script needs a dashboard or a dialog PowerShell SDK The same features as cmdlets, plus background tasks in isolated runspaces A PowerShell script needs a settings form or a small reactive UI PowerShell UI Add-NHKUi* components bound to New-NHKUiState values A shell pipeline needs the user to pick rows or fill a form CLI One command, stdin in, stdout out, exit status tells what happened

items.title: How they relate
items.text:
• The UI libraries are small layers built only on the public SDK of the same language. They do not wrap everything: native file dialogs, HTML <dialog>, clipboard, extra windows and live bitmaps are used through the SDK, next to the UI library, in the same app.
  • The CLI is a standalone program. It does not need Python or PowerShell, and scripts cannot subscribe to individual events; a window ends with one result.
  • You can start with the UI library and drop down to the SDK at any time: ui.document (Python) and the document of the window returned by Start-NHKUi (PowerShell) are ordinary SDK objects.

items.title: Rules of thumb
items.text:
• Prefer the SDK when the page is your own HTML/CSS design, when you show tables or logs, or when you need dialogs, several windows or bitmaps.
  • Prefer the UI library for settings, forms and small tools where state should drive the page automatically. It is an early (0.1.1) release; check its limitations.
  • Prefer the CLI when the rest of the program is a shell script and you need a single decision from the user.

Feature-by-feature availability is in the capability matrix.

items.title: CLI in five minutes
items.text: The nativehtmlkit command (alias nhk) shows a native window from any shell: pick rows (select), read text (view) or fill an HTML form (form). Input comes from stdin or a file, the result goes to stdout, and the exit status says what happened.

items.title: 1. Install
items.text:
Download the archive for your platform from the CLI releases (nativehtmlkit-cli-v0.1.2-linux-x64.tar.gz or nativehtmlkit-cli-v0.1.2-windows-x64.zip) and verify it against the release's SHA256SUMS before you run anything:

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing
tar xzf nativehtmlkit-cli-v0.1.2-linux-x64.tar.gz
export PATH="$PWD/nativehtmlkit-cli-v0.1.2-linux-x64:$PATH"
nativehtmlkit --version && nativehtmlkit doctor

The archive contains nativehtmlkit, the nhk alias, the bundled nativehtmlkit-host (Core 1.0.3), licences and an example form. Keep the files together: the CLI finds the host next to itself (or use --host PATH).

items.title: 2. Write hello-cli.sh
items.text:
examples/getting-started/hello-cli.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Hello, NativeHTMLKit CLI: ask the user to pick fruit in a native window.
#
# Teaches: piping lines into `nativehtmlkit select --multi` and reacting to its exit status.
# Run:     bash hello-cli.sh [--timeout SECONDS]
# Guide:   docs/getting-started/cli.md
set -euo pipefail
status=0
picked=$(printf '%s\n' apple banana cherry | nativehtmlkit select --multi --title "Pick fruit" "$@") || status=$?
case $status in
  0) echo "You picked:"; printf '%s\n' "$picked" | sed 's/^/  /' ;;
  2) echo "Cancelled" >&2 ;;
  124) echo "No answer in time" >&2 ;;
  *) echo "nativehtmlkit failed (exit $status)" >&2 ;;
esac
exit "$status"

items.title: 3. Run it
items.text:
bash hello-cli.sh
bash hello-cli.sh --timeout 10    # give up after ten seconds (exit status 124)

Real capture on KDE Plasma 6.6 Wayland with Core 1.0.3 and CLI 0.1.2.

items.title: Exit statuses
items.text:
Status Meaning 0 The user submitted (or closed a view); the selection is on stdout 1 Error (bad input, host problem); details on stderr 2 The user cancelled or closed the window 124 --timeout expired before the user decided 130 / 143 / 129 Interrupted by SIGINT / SIGTERM / SIGHUP

select writes the selection only on success, so a script can always trust stdout when the status is 0.

  • Button callbacks receive ($eventObject, $data), where $data is what you passed with -Data.
  • Start-NHKUi opens the window and (unless -NoReady) announces ready; you still run Wait-NativeHTMLKit -UntilShutdown yourself. Stop-NHKUi ends the bindings; dispose computed values with .Dispose().

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Start-NativeHTMLKitScript started the native host; the host ran hello.ps1 a second time, with the same PowerShell edition and arguments, and the call returned the connected application there. In the first run the script ends inside that call. Everything above it runs twice.
  • New-NativeHTMLKitWindow and Open-NativeHTMLKitHtml created the window and its document.
  • Register-NativeHTMLKitDocumentEvent subscribed a script block to clicks on #greet. Callbacks run later, inside Wait-NativeHTMLKit, on this same runspace. State that callbacks change is kept in an object ($counter.Clicks), because assigning a plain variable inside a script block only creates a local copy.
  • Set-NativeHTMLKitDocumentText changes text safely; it is never parsed as HTML.
  • Set-NativeHTMLKitReady announces startup is complete; Wait-NativeHTMLKit -UntilShutdown pumps events until the last window closes. Close-NativeHTMLKit in finally releases everything.

Short aliases exist for most commands (New-NHKWindow, Open-NHKHtml, Wait-NHK, ...). This site uses the full names.

items.title: Python UI in five minutes
items.text: nativehtmlkit_ui is a small reactive component library built on the public Python SDK. You describe the window with ui.heading(), ui.input(), ui.button() and friends; values that change are state() objects, and anything bound to them updates by itself. UI 0.1.1 is an early release.

items.text: python -m pip install nativehtmlkit_ui    # installs the nativehtmlkit SDK as a dependency

items.title: 2. Write hello_ui.py
items.text:
examples/getting-started/hello_ui.py
"""Hello, NativeHTMLKit UI: a reactive counter with nativehtmlkit_ui.

Teaches: state(), a text bound to a lambda, buttons, ui.mount(app), ui.dispose().
Run:     python hello_ui.py
Guide:   docs/getting-started/python-ui.md
"""
from nativehtmlkit import Application
from nativehtmlkit_ui import UI, state


def main():
    with Application.start(name="Counter") as app:
        count = state(0)
        ui = UI(title="Counter", theme="cobalt", density="regular", width=420, height=300)
        with ui.column():
            ui.heading("Counter", level=1)
            ui.text(lambda: f"Count: {count.value}")  # re-rendered whenever count changes
            with ui.row():
                ui.button("+1", on_click=lambda _e: count.set(count.value + 1))
                ui.button("Reset", variant="secondary", on_click=lambda _e: count.set(0))
        try:
            ui.mount(app)  # build the tree first, then mount it into a window
            app.run()
        finally:
            ui.dispose()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• state(0) is an observable value. count.set(...) changes it; reading count.value inside a lambda passed to ui.text() makes that text depend on it.
  • The with ui.column(): / with ui.row(): blocks build a tree. Build the whole tree before ui.mount(app); after mounting, change state instead of adding components.
  • ui.mount(app) opens the window through the SDK; app.run() is the same event loop as in the SDK quick start.
  • ui.dispose() releases bindings and the UI's owner thread.

Themes: cobalt (default), graphite, daylight; densities: compact, regular, comfortable. See Theme the UI library.
